units.intro: **Scarcity:** wants exceed what resources can make. That forces **choice**. The next-best thing you drop is **opportunity cost**. Economics studies how people, firms and governments choose under scarcity to satisfy material wants as well as they can.

cards.title: 1.0 Introduction to Economics
body: The choices that individuals and societies make in response to scarcity are the subject matter of economics.
Economics is the science of making choices with the objective to meet human wants as much as possible.
Economics is the study of how individuals and societies choose to use their scarce resources in order to satisfy their material wants as much as possible.
Economics is a social science concerned with the efficient use of limited (scarce) resources to achieve maximum satisfaction of human material wants.
Scarcity will always exist and cannot be eliminated in all societies; it is a universal economic problem.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A production possibilities curve that is concave (bowed outward) from the origin indicates which of the following?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand the shape of the PPC**
A concave (bowed-outward) PPC indicates that as you produce more of one good, the amount of the other good you must sacrifice increases.

**Step 2: Relate to the Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost**
This occurs because economic resources are specialized and not equally adaptable to the production of both goods.

**Step 3: Conclusion**
Therefore, a concave curve represents **increasing opportunity costs**.

cards.q: An entrepreneur starting a sole proprietorship faces which of the following legal financial characteristics?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define Sole Proprietorship characteristics**
A sole proprietorship is owned by a single individual. legally, there is no separation between the business entity and the personal owner.

**Step 2: Understand the liability consequences**
Because there is no legal separation, the owner faces **unlimited liability**, meaning personal assets can be seized to pay off business debts.

**Step 3: Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct answer is **Unlimited liability**.

cards.q: Which mode of transport is the most appropriate and cost-effective for moving extremely bulky, heavy, non-perishable goods across international borders?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Evaluate transportation mode constraints**
- Air: Fast, but very expensive and limited weight capacity.
- Road: Flexible, but restricted by land borders and low capacity per vehicle.
- Water: Slow, but lowest cost per unit and designed for huge bulk over long oceanic distances.

**Step 2: Conclusion**
For international, heavy, bulky, non-perishable cargo, **Water transportation** is the most cost-effective.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The historical Massawa-Asmara ropeway, constructed during the Italian colonial period, was dismantled by which authority?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the historical timeline of the Eritrean ropeway**
The $$71\text{ km}$$ ropeway was constructed during the Italian colonial period to connect the Port of Massawa with Asmara.

**Step 2: Identify when and by whom it was dismantled**
Following the defeat of Italy in World War II, the British took administration of Eritrea and dismantled the ropeway, selling it for scrap.

**Step 3: Select the correct option**
This corresponds to the **British Administration**.

glossary.meaning: Scarcity of resources is the inability of societies to produce enough goods and/or services to satisfy all their material wants and needs.
Economics is the science of making choices with the objective to meet human wants as much as possible.
Production is the transformation of inputs into outputs by business firms.
Human capital is the economic characterization of the education and training of workers.
Labour is the most active factor of production.
Opportunity cost is the amount of goods that must be sacrificed to obtain a unit of another good.
Wealth is the sum of all the assets accumulated over time by a society or a country.
Welfare is the state of well-being of a society.
Microeconomics is a branch of economics that studies the economic behavior of individual decisionmaking units such as consumers and business firms.
Corporation is a egal entity, distinct and separate from the individuals who own it.
Transportation is the safe movement of goods (freight) and people from one place to another.
Water transportation is the safe movement of goods and people through the routes of water bodies such ocean, sea, river, lake or canal.
Air transportation is the safe movement of goods and people from one place to another using air routes.
Communication is the transfer (or exchange) of any kind of information from one person or place to another person or place.
Communication system is a combination of processes and hardware (instruments) used to accomplish the transfer of information (communication).

units.title: Money and Financial Institutions
units.intro:
Barter needs a double coincidence of wants. Money kills that problem. Functions: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value (and sometimes standard of deferred payment). Good money is durable, portable, divisible, scarce, acceptable.

Banks take deposits, keep a fraction as reserve, lend the rest — that is how credit multiplies (school picture). Central bank (or the state’s bank) issues notes, holds reserves, tries to keep the currency trusted. Other institutions: insurance, microfinance, savings groups — the book’s local list.

glossary.meaning: Barter is the exchange of goods for goods without the use of money.

Pooling is the spreading of losses incurred by the few over the entire group, so that in the process, average loss is substituted for actual loss.

cards.title: 3.1 Starting an Accounting System and The Accounting Equation (1/3)
body: **Accounting** is the art of planning, identifying, measuring, recording, summarizing, interpreting, and analyzing financial transactions to provide reliable, stated-in-money (Nakfa) information to assist users in making informed economic decisions. While accounting covers a wide range of analytical activities, **Bookkeeping** is the systematic recording of day-to-day financial transactions. It is a vital branch of accounting, often described as 'one slice of the *Hmbasha* (traditional bread) that is accounting.' Accounting information serves both internal users (such as business owners, managers, and employees) and external users (including bankers, suppliers, government tax agencies, and auditors).

Service rendering businesses, such as hotels, garages, and transportation firms (e.g., taxi or minibus operations), generate revenue by performing intangible actions for customers rather than selling physical merchandise. For any business to set up a logical record-keeping framework, it must first determine its starting financial position. A person's or business's financial worth is determined by looking at what they own (assets) and what they owe (debts or liabilities). Subtracting what is owed from what is owned reveals the owner's net worth or capital.
This relationship is formally expressed through the fundamental **Accounting Equation**:
$$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Capital}$$

cards.title: 3.1 Starting an Accounting System and The Accounting Equation (2/3)
body: **Assets** are economic resources of value owned or controlled by a business that are expected to provide future economic benefits (e.g., cash, accounts receivable, supplies, equipment, land, and buildings). **Liabilities** are debts or financial obligations owed by the business to external creditors (e.g., accounts payable, salaries payable, taxes payable, and mortgage payable). **Capital** (or owner's equity) represents the owner's residual claim on the assets after all liabilities have been settled.

To report the starting financial worth of a business on a specific date, accountants prepare a **Balance Sheet**. The balance sheet has a structural heading consisting of three lines: the name of the business, the name of the financial form (Balance Sheet), and the specific date of the statement. The body of the balance sheet is divided into two balanced sections: assets are listed on the left-hand side, while liabilities and capital are listed on the right-hand side, illustrating that the two sides must always be mathematically equal.

Classification — Balance Sheet Side — Account Examples — Economic Meaning | Assets — Left-hand side — Cash, Supplies, Automobiles, Land — Useful resources owned by the business | Liabilities — Right-hand side — Accounts Payable, Taxes Payable — Obligations owed to external creditors | Capital — Right-hand side — Owner's Capital, Retained Earnings — Residual interest owned by the proprietor

> **💡 Did You Know?**: The balance sheet is called a 'snapshot' of a business because it captures the exact financial condition of the enterprise at one specific moment in time, such as the close of business on September 1. By the next day, transactions will have already changed the balances!

cards.title: 3.2 Transaction Analysis and Double-Entry Rules (1/2)
body: **Transaction Analysis** is the process of studying a business transaction to determine its dual effect on the basic elements of the accounting equation, identifying which accounts are affected, their classification, and whether they increase or decrease. Every transaction must be analyzed in terms of its impact on the equation $$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Capital}$$ before it is entered into the records. This ensures that the accounting equation remains in balance after every single transaction.

Accounting systems are governed by **Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP)**, which provide standard guidelines for financial reporting. Three core principles are: • **The Historical Cost Principle:** Dictates that assets must be recorded in the accounting records at the exact price paid to acquire them, and this cost remains unchanged regardless of market fluctuations. • **The Objectivity Principle:** Requires that all accounting records be based on objective, verifiable evidence supported by source documents (e.g., invoices, receipts, and cheque stubs) rather than personal opinions. • **The Business Entity Concept:** States that a business must be treated as a separate and distinct economic unit from its owner(s) and any other business.

Modern accounting uses **Double-Entry Bookkeeping**, which means that every transaction affects at least two accounts. One account is debited, and another is credited. The term **Debit** (abbreviated as Dr.) refers to the left-hand side of any account, while **Credit** (abbreviated as Cr.) refers to the right-hand side. The normal balance of an account is on the side where increases are recorded.

cards.title: 3.2 Transaction Analysis and Double-Entry Rules (2/2)
body: To demonstrate these changes, accountants use a simplified ledger account known as a **T-Account**. The basic rules of debit and credit are structured around the accounting equation: • **Asset Accounts:** Increased by debits (left side) and decreased by credits (right side). Their normal balance is a debit. • **Liability Accounts:** Decreased by debits (left side) and increased by credits (right side). Their normal balance is a credit. • **Capital Accounts:** Decreased by debits (left side) and increased by credits (right side). Their normal balance is a credit.

Account Type — Increase Side — Decrease Side — Normal Balance Side | Asset — Debit (Left) — Credit (Right) — Debit (Left) | Liability — Credit (Right) — Debit (Left) — Credit (Right) | Capital — Credit (Right) — Debit (Left) — Credit (Right) | Revenue — Credit (Right) — Debit (Left) — Credit (Right) | Expense / Drawing — Debit (Left) — Credit (Right) — Debit (Left)

> **💡 Did You Know?**: The formalization of double-entry bookkeeping is credited to Luca Pacioli, an Italian Franciscan monk and mathematician, who published the first systematic description of the system in Venice in 1494. He used the terms *Dr.* (from the Italian *debito*, meaning 'owed to the proprietor') and *Cr.* (from *credito*, meaning 'trust' or 'belief' in the proprietor).

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: To easily memorize debit and credit rules, use the acronym **A-E-D**: **A**ssets, **E**xpenses, and **D**rawings are all increased by debits. All other accounts (Liabilities, Capital, and Revenue) are increased by credits.

cards.title: 3.3 Journalizing and Posting (General and Special Journals) (1/2)
body: **Journalizing** is the process of recording business transactions in chronological order (by date) in a book of original entry called a **Journal**. The journal provides an orderly, complete history of all transactions, showing both the debit and credit effects of each transaction in one place. This reduces errors and makes it easier to verify that debits equal credits before transactions are transferred to individual ledger accounts. The simplest form of journal is the **General Journal**, which has two amount columns: a left-hand column for debits and a right-hand column for credits.

For businesses with a high volume of repetitive cash transactions, using only a general journal is inefficient because it requires posting each entry individually. To save time and space, businesses use **Special Journals**, such as a **Cash Journal**. A cash journal contains specialized columns for frequently debited or credited accounts (e.g., Cash Debit, Cash Credit, and Fares Earned Credit). Transactions that do not involve cash (such as buying equipment on credit) are recorded separately in the general journal.

Once transactions are recorded in a journal, they must be posted. **Posting** is the systematic process of transferring debits and credits from the journal (the book of original entry) to the proper accounts in the **Ledger** (the book of secondary entry). The ledger organizes all transactions by account, making it easy to determine the current balance of any asset, liability, or capital item.

To ensure the accuracy of the journalizing process, accountants perform **Footing**—adding up the debit and credit columns on a journal page to verify that the totals are equal. During posting, cross-referencing is maintained by writing the journal page number in the Post Reference (P.R.) column of the ledger, and the ledger account number in the P.R. column of the journal. This establishes an audit trail for verification.

> **💡 Did You Know?**: In accounting, the Post Reference (P.R.) column in the journal is left blank until the posting is actually completed. If you see a number in the P.R. column, it acts as a visual signal that the amount has been successfully transferred to the ledger!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: When using a special cash journal, do not post individual entries in the cash columns daily. Instead, post only the **column totals** at the end of the month. This simple step can reduce your posting labor by up to $$90\%$$!

cards.title: 3.4 The Trial Balance and The Work Sheet (1/3)
body: **The Trial Balance** is a two-column list of all ledger accounts and their current balances at a specific date, with debit balances placed in the left-hand column and credit balances placed in the right-hand column. Its primary purpose is to prove the mathematical equality of total debits and total credits in the ledger after posting. A trial balance is prepared at regular intervals, typically at the end of a monthly or annual **fiscal period**.

While a balancing trial balance indicates that total debits equal total credits, it does not guarantee that the accounting records are error-free. It cannot detect errors such as completely omitting a transaction, recording a transaction twice, posting a correct amount to the wrong account of the same type, or **transposition errors** (reversing the order of digits, like writing Nakfa $$12$$ as Nakfa $$21$$) if the error affects both sides equally.

To organize financial data and plan adjustments at the end of a fiscal period, accountants prepare a **Work Sheet**. An **Eight-Column Work Sheet** contains pairs of debit and credit columns for: 1. **Trial Balance:** The unadjusted ledger balances. 2. **Adjustments:** Updates to accounts to reflect current values. 3. **Income Statement:** Revenues and expenses used to compute net income. 4. **Balance Sheet:** Assets, liabilities, and capital balances.

**Adjusting Entries** are journal entries made at the end of a fiscal period to update accounts to reflect revenues earned and expenses incurred during the period (matching principle). Two common adjustments for a service business are: • **Supplies Adjustment:** Supplies are recorded as assets when purchased. As they are used, they become an expense. At the end of the period, a physical count is taken to determine the value of supplies remaining on hand. The value of supplies used (supplies expense) is calculated as:

cards.title: 3.4 The Trial Balance and The Work Sheet (2/3)
body: $$\text{Supplies Expense} = \text{Beginning Supplies Balance} - \text{Supplies on Hand (Physical Count)}$$

• **Depreciation Adjustment:** Fixed assets (e.g., automobiles or office equipment) provide services over many years. **Depreciation** is the systematic process of allocating the cost of a fixed asset as an expense over its useful life. The monthly depreciation expense is calculated as:
$$\text{Monthly Depreciation} = \frac{\text{Cost of Asset}}{\text{Total Useful Life (in Months)}}$$
To preserve the historical cost of the asset, depreciation is credited to a contra-asset account called **Accumulated Depreciation**, which is deducted from the asset account on the balance sheet.

cards.title: 3.5 Financial Statements and Closing the Ledger (1/3)
body: **Financial Statements** are the structured reports that a business prepares at the end of a fiscal period to communicate its financial performance and position to interested users. A complete set of financial statements for a service business includes: • **The Income Statement:** Reports the profitability of the business over a period of time by matching revenues (e.g., fares earned) against expenses (e.g., salary, rent, utilities, and depreciation). If revenues exceed expenses, a **Net Income** is generated; if expenses exceed revenues, a **Net Loss** occurs. • **The Capital Statement (Owner's Equity Statement):** Summarizes the changes in the owner's capital during the fiscal period. It is calculated as:
$$\text{Ending Capital} = \text{Beginning Capital} + \text{Net Income} - \text{Owner's Drawings}$$
• **The Balance Sheet:** Reports the financial position of the business on a specific date, presenting assets (with contra-asset accounts deducted), liabilities, and the updated ending capital.

At the end of the fiscal period, the accounting cycle is completed by **Closing the Books**. This process prepares the accounts for the next period by distinguishing between: 1. **Permanent (Real) Accounts:** Accounts that appear on the balance sheet (assets, liabilities, and capital). Their balances carry forward to the next period and are **never** closed. 2. **Temporary (Nominal) Accounts:** Accounts that appear on the income statement (revenues and expenses) and the owner's drawing account. Their balances must be reduced to zero at the end of each period so they do not mix with the next period's data.

cards.title: 3.5 Financial Statements and Closing the Ledger (2/3)
body: **Closing Entries** are journal entries that transfer the balances of temporary accounts to a temporary clearing account called **Income Summary**, and then to the owner's capital account. The closing process involves four steps: • **Step 1: Close Revenue Accounts:** Debit each revenue account for its balance, and credit **Income Summary**. • **Step 2: Close Expense Accounts:** Debit **Income Summary** for total expenses, and credit each individual expense account. • **Step 3: Close Income Summary:** Debit **Income Summary** for the net income (or credit for a net loss), and credit/debit the owner's **Capital** account. • **Step 4: Close the Drawing Account:** Debit the owner's **Capital** account, and credit the **Drawing** account.

Once closing entries are posted, a **Post-Closing Trial Balance** is prepared. It contains only permanent (balance sheet) accounts with non-zero balances, verifying that the ledger remains in balance and is ready for the next fiscal period.

Account Category — Account Type — Closed At Year-End? — Post-Closing Trial Balance? | Permanent — Assets, Liabilities, Capital — No — Yes (non-zero balances) | Temporary — Revenues, Expenses — Yes (to Income Summary) — No (balance is zero) | Temporary — Owner's Drawing — Yes (directly to Capital) — No (balance is zero)

> **💡 Did You Know?**: The Income Summary account is a unique temporary account that exists for only a few minutes during the year-end closing process. It is opened, used to compute the net income or loss, closed to capital, and left with a zero balance until the next year-end!

tips.text: From time to time, the owner of a business wants to know how well his/her business is doing.
An owner wants to know if he/she is profiting or losing money.
In order to determine whether a business operation has resulted in net profit or net loss, every business transaction is recorded in a journal.

Prior to journalizing, business transactions are analysed using a financial transaction work sheet to determine the transactions effect on the accounting equation and facilitate recording journal entries.

In this sub-unit, we illustrated the analysis of business transactions such as: additional investment of capital by the owner of the business; purchase of an asset for cash; purchase of an asset on account; part payment of a liability; sale of an asset for cash; income transactions and expense transactions.
In the following sub-unit, we will record the business transactions in a General Journal.

The use of a cash journal in service business helps to save space and time in recording and posting entries. Moreover, it helps in proving the cash on hand.
